content:
Quick answer: Living with arthritis can affect pain, stiffness, fatigue, sleep, movement, mood, work and everyday activities. Arthritis is not one single condition, so experiences vary. Helpful support may include suitable movement, pacing, sleep support, treatment discussions and practical adjustments.

There is no single way that arthritis feels or affects daily life. Some people have symptoms in one joint, while others have inflammation, fatigue or symptoms affecting several parts of life. This guide explains common experiences and practical questions to discuss with a GP, pharmacist, physiotherapist or rheumatology team.

What can living with arthritis feel like?

  • pain or tenderness in one or more joints
  • stiffness after waking or sitting still
  • swelling, warmth or reduced movement
  • fatigue that makes ordinary tasks harder
  • sleep disrupted by pain or stiffness
  • less confidence with walking, stairs, work or social activities
  • low mood or frustration when symptoms change from day to day

These symptoms can have different causes. Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout and other conditions need different assessment and treatment. A symptom pattern alone cannot confirm a diagnosis.

How arthritis can affect an ordinary day

Morning and getting moving

Some people notice stiffness or pain when getting out of bed. Gentle movement, time to get ready and an agreed exercise plan may help. If morning stiffness is new, prolonged or worsening, discuss it with a healthcare professional.

Work, caring and household tasks

Arthritis may make lifting, typing, standing, driving, dressing or concentrating more difficult. Breaking tasks into smaller parts, changing position regularly and asking about reasonable workplace adjustments can help. Benefits and work-support decisions depend on individual circumstances.

Evenings, sleep and fatigue

Pain and worry can disturb sleep, while poor sleep can make pain and fatigue harder to manage. Keep a simple record of sleep, symptoms and activity, and ask for help if fatigue is severe, new or interfering with safety and daily care.

Movement, pacing and flare planning

Many people benefit from regular, suitable activity, but the right amount depends on the condition, symptoms and general health. Start gradually, avoid sudden increases and ask a qualified professional how to adapt movement if a joint becomes hot, sharply more painful or swollen.

  • plan important activities for the time of day when you have most energy
  • alternate activity with planned rests instead of waiting until exhausted
  • use gentle range-of-motion or low-impact activity where appropriate
  • keep a flare plan with agreed medicines and contact details
  • avoid changing or stopping prescribed medicines without advice

Explore our arthritis exercise hub, flare-up guidance and arthritis pain-relief guide for related information.

Living with different types of arthritis

Osteoarthritis often involves pain and stiffness related to use and joint change. Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis may involve swelling, prolonged stiffness, fatigue and symptoms beyond the joints. Gout can cause sudden, severe attacks in a joint. The right diagnosis matters because treatment and monitoring differ.

Read more about osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and arthritis generally.

When to seek medical advice

Arrange medical advice if joint pain, stiffness, swelling or fatigue is new, worsening, limiting daily activities or not settling. A GP, pharmacist, physiotherapist or specialist team can help decide what assessment and treatment are appropriate.

Seek urgent advice from NHS 111 or an urgent GP service if a joint is hot and swollen and you feel feverish, shivery or generally unwell. Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency, severe breathing difficulty, collapse, or sudden neurological symptoms.

Questions to take to an appointment

  • What could be causing my symptoms?
  • What movement or exercise is suitable for me?
  • How should I manage a flare?
  • Could medicines, sleep, mood or another condition be contributing?
  • Would physiotherapy, occupational therapy or other support help?
  • What symptoms should prompt urgent help?

Frequently asked questions

Can people live well with arthritis?

Many people find ways to manage arthritis and continue activities that matter to them. It may take time to find the right combination of treatment, movement, pacing and practical support.

Should I exercise if I have arthritis?

Suitable activity often forms part of arthritis self-management, but the type and amount should match your health and symptoms. Stop and seek advice if exercise causes marked or persistent worsening.

Can arthritis affect mood?

Long-term pain, fatigue, sleep disruption and uncertainty can affect mood. Speak to a GP or another healthcare professional if low mood, anxiety or hopelessness is persistent or affecting daily life.

Where can I find UK arthritis support?

Start with your GP, NHS 111 when urgent advice is needed, your pharmacist, physiotherapy services or rheumatology team. You can also explore our Benefits and PIP hub and self-help resources.
